Title: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus
Author: Mary Shelley
First published: London, 1818 (anonymous); revised edition 1831.
Form: Epistolary frame narrative told through the letters of Arctic explorer Robert Walton, who encounters Victor Frankenstein during an expedition.
Plot facts:
- Victor Frankenstein, a Genevan student of natural philosophy, assembles and animates a creature from dead matter.
- The creature is rejected by its creator and by the society that recoils from its appearance.
- The creature turns against Frankenstein; the two become bound in a mutual pursuit that drives the plot.
Context:
- Widely treated as an early example of science fiction.
- Themes: ambition, responsibility, isolation, and what an inventor owes to the life he brings into being.
Excerpt: "It was on a dreary night of November that I beheld the accomplishment of my toils... I saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open."

Title: Dracula
Author: Bram Stoker (Irish author)
First published: London, 1897.
Form: Epistolary novel assembled from letters, diary entries, and newspaper clippings rather than a single continuous narration.
Plot facts:
- Count Dracula, a vampire from Transylvania, relocates to England.
- The solicitor Jonathan Harker travels to the Count's castle on business as the novel opens.
- A group led by Professor Abraham Van Helsing forms to oppose the vampire and protect those he targets.
Context:
- Credited with helping define the modern vampire genre.
- Engages period anxieties about foreign invasion and the spread of disease.
- The layered documentary structure lets several narrators assemble one account from fragments.
Excerpt: "I am all in a sea of wonders. I doubt; I fear; I think strange things, which I dare not confess to my own soul."

Title: Moby-Dick; or, The Whale
Author: Herman Melville
First published: 1851.
Narration: A sailor who introduces himself with the words "Call me Ishmael."
Plot facts:
- The whaling ship Pequod sails under Captain Ahab.
- Ahab is consumed by his pursuit of a white sperm whale named Moby Dick that had maimed him on an earlier voyage.
- The novel interleaves the chase with extended digressions on the practice and science of whaling.
Context:
- Early reviews were mixed and the book sold modestly during Melville's lifetime.
- Now regarded as a major work of American literature, frequently studied for its blend of adventure, encyclopedic detail, and philosophical inquiry.
Excerpt: "Whenever I find myself growing grim about the mouth... then I account it high time to get to sea as soon as I can."

Title: Pride and Prejudice
Author: Jane Austen
First published: 1813.
Setting: Among the landed gentry of early nineteenth-century England.
Plot facts:
- Elizabeth Bennet is the second of five sisters whose family's circumstances make advantageous marriage a pressing question.
- The narrative traces Elizabeth's changing relationship with Mr. Darcy, a wealthy and reserved gentleman.
- The initial misjudgements each forms about the other are gradually corrected.
Context:
- Known for its irony and its commentary on the social conventions governing courtship and class.
- Recurring concerns: marriage, economic security, reputation, first impressions, and family standing.
Excerpt: "It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife."

Title: Jane Eyre
Author: Charlotte Bronte (originally published under the pen name Currer Bell)
First published: 1847.
Form: First-person bildungsroman.
Plot facts:
- Jane Eyre, an orphan, endures a harsh childhood at Gateshead and the austere Lowood school before taking a post as governess at Thornfield Hall.
- She falls in love with her employer, Edward Rochester, whose house holds a hidden secret.
- Jane leaves Thornfield to preserve her principles and later returns on changed terms.
Context:
- Notable for its assertion of the moral and spiritual independence of its narrator.
- Themes: conscience, social class, religion, and the struggle for autonomy.
Excerpt: "I am no bird; and no net ensnares me: I am a free human being with an independent will."

Title: The Great Gatsby
Author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
First published: 1925.
Setting: Long Island and New York City during the Jazz Age.
Narration: Told by Nick Carraway, a Midwesterner who moves east and rents a cottage next to a mansion.
Plot facts:
- Jay Gatsby, a wealthy man of mysterious origin, throws lavish parties in pursuit of his lost love, Daisy Buchanan.
- Nick observes the entanglement of Gatsby, Daisy, and her husband Tom, which moves toward tragedy.
Context:
- Often read as a portrait of the American Dream and its disillusionment.
- Themes: wealth, class, longing, and the gap between aspiration and reality.
Excerpt: "So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past."

Title: War and Peace
Author: Leo Tolstoy
First published: serialized 1865-1867, complete 1869.
Scope: A long historical novel set in Russia during the Napoleonic Wars.
Plot facts:
- Follows several aristocratic families, among them the Bezukhovs, Bolkonskys, and Rostovs, across war and domestic life.
- Pierre Bezukhov, Prince Andrei Bolkonsky, and Natasha Rostova are central figures whose lives are reshaped by the 1812 French invasion.
- The narrative alternates between battlefield events and the private concerns of its characters.
Context:
- Famous for its scale and for Tolstoy's reflections on history and the limits of individual agency.
- Themes: history, fate, family, and the search for meaning.
Excerpt: "We can know only that we know nothing. And that is the highest degree of human wisdom."

Title: Crime and Punishment
Author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
First published: serialized 1866.
Setting: Saint Petersburg.
Plot facts:
- Rodion Raskolnikov, an impoverished former student, murders a pawnbroker, convinced he is exempt from ordinary moral law.
- The act plunges him into guilt, paranoia, and illness as the investigator Porfiry Petrovich closes in.
- His relationship with Sonia, a young woman driven to prostitution by poverty, moves him toward confession.
Context:
- A psychological novel examining conscience, suffering, and redemption.
- Themes: guilt, free will, alienation, and moral responsibility.
Excerpt: "Pain and suffering are always inevitable for a large intelligence and a deep heart."

Title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
Author: Mark Twain (pen name of Samuel Clemens)
First published: 1884 (UK), 1885 (US).
Narration: First-person, in Huck's vernacular voice.
Plot facts:
- Huckleberry Finn flees his abusive father and his "civilizing" guardians and travels down the Mississippi River on a raft.
- He journeys with Jim, a man escaping enslavement, and the two form a bond as they encounter swindlers and danger along the river.
Context:
- Noted for its use of regional dialect and its satire of pre-Civil-War Southern society.
- Themes: freedom, conscience, race, and the tension between social convention and individual morality.
Excerpt: "All right, then, I'll go to hell."

Title: Wuthering Heights
Author: Emily Bronte (originally published under the pen name Ellis Bell)
First published: 1847.
Form: Frame narrative related through the housekeeper Nelly Dean to the tenant Mr. Lockwood.
Setting: The Yorkshire moors.
Plot facts:
- The intense, destructive bond between Catherine Earnshaw and the foundling Heathcliff shapes two generations of the Earnshaw and Linton families.
- Heathcliff's thwarted love turns to a long campaign of revenge against both households.
Context:
- Distinctive for its nested narration and its bleak moorland atmosphere.
- Themes: obsessive love, revenge, class, and the persistence of the past.
Excerpt: "Whatever our souls are made of, his and mine are the same."
